results.name: outlier_vs_majority_neighbour
results.description: In 3-4 example sets where all but one example share a final digit, yes-rate for non-example targets within 3 of the outlier example minus yes-rate for off-digit non-example targets within 3 of a majority example (and not near the outlier); observed above the null means people favour the outlier's neighbourhood even more than the anchored-exception model, below means the model over-produces it.
results.code:
# name: outlier_vs_majority_neighbour
# description: In 3-4 example sets where all but one example share a final digit, yes-rate for non-example targets within 3 of the outlier example minus yes-rate for off-digit non-example targets within 3 of a majority example (and not near the outlier); observed above the null means people favour the outlier's neighbourhood even more than the anchored-exception model, below means the model over-produces it.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    D = np.where(np.isnan(E), np.nan, np.mod(E, 10))
    # count of examples sharing each example's final digit
    same = np.sum(D[:, :, None] == D[:, None, :], axis=2).astype(float)
    same[np.isnan(D)] = np.nan
    is_out = (same == 1) & ((np.nan_to_num(same, nan=0) == 1).sum(axis=1)[:, None] == 1) & (np.nanmax(same, axis=1)[:, None] == (n - 1)[:, None])
    valid = (n >= 3) & is_out.any(axis=1)
    out_val = np.nansum(np.where(is_out, E, 0.0), axis=1)
    maj_digit = np.nansum(np.where(~is_out & ~np.isnan(E), D, 0.0), axis=1) / np.maximum(n - 1, 1)
    maj = np.where(~is_out & ~np.isnan(E), E, np.nan)
    d_out = np.abs(t - out_val)
    d_maj = np.nanmin(np.abs(maj - t[:, None]), axis=1) if valid.any() else np.full(len(t), np.inf)
    d_maj = np.where(np.isnan(d_maj), np.inf, d_maj)
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    off = np.mod(t, 10) != maj_digit
    a = valid & ~is_ex & (d_out <= 3) & off
    b = valid & ~is_ex & (d_maj <= 3) & (d_out > 3) & off
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: trial_drift_residual
results.description: Pearson correlation between trial_index and the rating's residual from its (set, target) cell mean; observed negative vs a null near zero means people say yes less often later in the session (a drift the stationary model lacks).

results.name: partial_final_digit_match
results.description: In sets of 3-4 examples with at least two distinct final digits, yes-rate for non-example targets sharing their final digit with exactly one example; observed above the null means people generalize from single examples' final digits ("seen final digits") more than the model's one-rule-plus-exception account allows.
results.code:
# name: partial_final_digit_match
# description: In sets of 3-4 examples with at least two distinct final digits, yes-rate for non-example targets sharing their final digit with exactly one example; observed above the null means people generalize from single examples' final digits ("seen final digits") more than the model's one-rule-plus-exception account allows.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    D = np.where(np.isnan(E), -1.0, np.mod(E, 10))
    # distinct final digits per row (vectorised over the 4 columns)
    Ds = np.sort(D, axis=1)
    distinct = (Ds[:, 0] >= 0).astype(int) + np.sum((np.diff(Ds, axis=1) != 0) & (Ds[:, 1:] >= 0), axis=1)
    matches = np.sum(D == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None], axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    m = (n >= 3) & (distinct >= 2) & (matches == 1) & ~is_ex
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].to_numpy()[m].mean())

results.name: first_vs_last_example_proximity
results.description: In 2-4 example sets, yes-rate for non-example targets within 10 of the first-shown example (and farther from the last) minus yes-rate for targets within 10 of the last-shown example (and farther from the first); nonzero observed vs a model null means presentation order matters (positive = primacy), which the order-blind model cannot produce.
results.code:
# name: first_vs_last_example_proximity
# description: In 2-4 example sets, yes-rate for non-example targets within 10 of the first-shown example (and farther from the last) minus yes-rate for targets within 10 of the last-shown example (and farther from the first); nonzero observed vs a model null means presentation order matters (positive = primacy), which the order-blind model cannot produce.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    last = E[np.arange(len(E)), np.maximum(n - 1, 0)]
    first = E[:, 0]
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    df1 = np.abs(t - first); dl = np.abs(t - last)
    base = (n >= 2) & ~is_ex
    a = base & (df1 <= 10) & (dl > 10)
    b = base & (dl <= 10) & (df1 > 10)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: single_example_generalization
results.description: Yes-rate on non-example targets for single-example sets; observed above the null means people generalize more broadly from one example than the model's size-principle posterior predicts, below means more narrowly.
results.code:
# name: single_example_generalization
# description: Yes-rate on non-example targets for single-example sets; observed above the null means people generalize more broadly from one example than the model's size-principle posterior predicts, below means more narrowly.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~s.str.contains(",")
    ex = pd.to_numeric(s.where(single, "-1"), errors="coerce").to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    m = single.to_numpy() & (ex != t)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].to_numpy()[m].mean())

results.name: cell_unanimity
results.description: Fraction of (set, target) cells whose responses are all identical (all yes or all no); observed above the null means people's judgments are more deterministic/consensual than the model's graded probabilities, below means more mixed.

results.name: shown_example_endorsement
results.description: Yes-rate on trials whose target is one of the shown examples, in sets of 2-4 examples; observed below the model's null means people reject shown examples (esp. outliers) more than the model, which nearly always includes them in the concept.
results.code:
# name: shown_example_endorsement
# description: Yes-rate on trials whose target is one of the shown examples, in sets of 2-4 examples; observed below the model's null means people reject shown examples (esp. outliers) more than the model, which nearly always includes them in the concept.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    m = is_ex & (n >= 2)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].to_numpy()[m].mean())

results.name: near_vs_far_offdigit_gradient
results.description: In 2-4 example sets, among non-example targets sharing no final digit with any example, yes-rate for targets within 5 of the nearest example minus yes-rate for targets more than 20 from every example; observed above the null means people's magnitude-similarity generalization is steeper/stronger than the model's intervals and neighbourhoods produce.
results.code:
# name: near_vs_far_offdigit_gradient
# description: In 2-4 example sets, among non-example targets sharing no final digit with any example, yes-rate for targets within 5 of the nearest example minus yes-rate for targets more than 20 from every example; observed above the null means people's magnitude-similarity generalization is steeper/stronger than the model's intervals and neighbourhoods produce.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    dig = np.any(np.mod(E, 10) == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None], axis=1)
    base = (n >= 2) & ~dig & (dist > 0)
    a = base & (dist <= 5)
    b = base & (dist > 20)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
